Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Bush signed an executive order Friday expanding U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe, the White House said. About 200 victims of election violence seek safety outside the U.S. Embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe, this month. "The new executive order significantly enhances our ability to designate individuals in and entities connected to the Mugabe regime," Bush said in a written statement that calls the Zimbabwean government under president Robert Mugabe "illegitimate." Just after the announcement, the Treasury Department said it has designated for sanctions 17 entities, including three government-owned or controlled companies used by Mugabe and his government "to illegally siphon revenue and foreign exchange from the Zimbabwean people," as well as one individual. "This action is a direct result of the Mugabe regime's continued politically motivated violence, disregarding calls from the Southern African Development Community, the African Union and the United Nations to halt the attacks," the White House said. "The regime has also continued its ban against NGO activities that would provide assistance to the suffering and vulnerable people of Zimbabwe. No regime should ignore the will of its own people and calls from the international community without consequences." The U.S. has been pushing for sanctions against Zimbabwe since Mugabe ignored a U.N. Security Council appeal to postpone a presidential runoff election June 27. The vote initially was intended to be a runoff between Mugabe and opposition candidate Morgan Tsvangirai, who did not win the presidency outright in the general election, according to government tallies. But Tsvangirai, of the Movement for Democratic Change, withdrew just before the vote, saying Mugabe's supporters had orchestrated a campaign of beatings, intimidation and murders against Tsvangirai supporters. Earlier this month, Russia and China vetoed a Security Council resolution pushed by the United States, Britain and France that would have imposed international sanctions on Mugabe and senior members of his government. Bush said last week he was "displeased" at the vetoes, but the Treasury and State Departments were working on potential U.S. action. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Jendayi Frazer told members of Congress last week that more than 100 people have been murdered, more than 3,000 have been injured by beatings or torture and more than 30,000 have been driven from their homes because of violence that broke out after the general election. Entities designated by the Treasury Department include Minerals Marketing Corp. of Zimbabwe, the company that serves as the sole marketing and export agent for all minerals mined in Zimbabwe except gold and silver; Zimbabwe Mining Development Corp.; and Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Co., among others. The individual named is Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari. The Treasury Department said he is an Omani national who has close ties to Mugabe and his top officials and uses his company, Oryx Natural Resources, to "enable Mugabe ... to maintain access to, and derive personal benefit from, various mining ventures in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Under the sanctions, any assets tied to al-Shanfari or to the designated companies that are within U.S. jurisdictions must be frozen, and people living in the United States are prohibited from doing business with them. On Monday, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed an agreement that paves the way for power-sharing talks to take place in the next few weeks. They will be mediated by South African President Thabo Mbeki, as a representative of the Southern African Development Community, and Jean Ping, chairman of the African Union Commission. Bush said Friday the United States is ready to provide a "substantial assistance package, development aid and normalization with international financial institutions" should those talks result in a new government "that reflects the will of the Zimbabwean people." In the meantime, the president said he is authorizing the use of up to $2.5 million from the U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to assist Zimbabwean refugees and those displaced by the violence. In addition, he said the United States will continue efforts to provide food and medical care to Zimbabweans.

**WASHINGTON** — President George W. Bush has signed an executive order expanding U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe, according to a White House announcement. The action comes as approximately 200 victims of political violence have sought refuge outside the U.S. Embassy in Harare this month. 

In an official statement characterizing the administration of President Robert Mugabe as "illegitimate," President Bush noted that the new executive order "significantly enhances our ability to designate individuals in and entities connected to the Mugabe regime." Shortly following the announcement, the U.S. Department of the Treasury designated 17 entities and one individual for targeted economic sanctions. Among these targets are three government-owned or controlled corporations utilized by Mugabe and his officials "to illegally siphon revenue and foreign exchange from the Zimbabwean people."

"This action is a direct result of the Mugabe regime's continued politically motivated violence, disregarding calls from the Southern African Development Community, the African Union and the United Nations to halt the attacks," the White House stated. "The regime has also continued its ban against NGO activities that would provide assistance to the suffering and vulnerable people of Zimbabwe. No regime should ignore the will of its own people and calls from the international community without consequences."

Washington has been pressing for international sanctions since Mugabe defied a U.N. Security Council appeal to postpone the June 27 presidential runoff election. Official tallies from the initial general election indicated that neither Mugabe nor opposition candidate Morgan Tsvangirai secured an outright majority. However, Tsvangirai, leader of the Movement for Democratic Change, withdrew prior to the runoff, asserting that Mugabe supporters had orchestrated a systematic campaign of violence, intimidation, beatings, and murders targeting opposition members.

Earlier this month, Russia and China vetoed a U.N. Security Council resolution—sponsored by the United States, Great Britain, and France—that would have imposed global sanctions on Mugabe and senior members of his administration. Although President Bush expressed strong displeasure over the vetoes, the State and Treasury Departments continued to formulate targeted U.S. measures. Highlighting the humanitarian crisis, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Jendayi Frazer informed members of Congress last week that post-election violence had claimed over 100 lives, left more than 3,000 people injured through beatings or torture, and displaced upwards of 30,000 individuals.

The entities sanctioned by the Treasury Department include the Minerals Marketing Corp. of Zimbabwe—which serves as the sole marketing and export agent for all minerals mined in the country, excluding gold and silver—as well as the Zimbabwe Mining Development Corp. and the Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Co., among others. 

The sanctioned individual was identified as Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari, an Omani national reported to maintain close ties with Mugabe and top leadership. According to the Treasury Department, al-Shanfari utilized his firm, Oryx Natural Resources, to "enable Mugabe ... to maintain access to, and derive personal benefit from, various mining ventures in the Democratic Republic of the Congo." Under the terms of the sanctions, any assets belonging to al-Shanfari or the designated entities within U.S. jurisdiction must be frozen, and U.S. persons are strictly prohibited from conducting business transactions with them.

Amid these escalating measures, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed an agreement on Monday establishing a framework for power-sharing negotiations set to take place over the coming weeks. These talks will be mediated by South African President Thabo Mbeki, representing the Southern African Development Community, alongside Jean Ping, Chairman of the African Union Commission. 

President Bush stated on Friday that the United States stands prepared to offer a "substantial assistance package, development aid and normalization with international financial institutions," provided the negotiations produce a legitimate government "that reflects the will of the Zimbabwean people." 

In the interim, the President authorized up to $2.5 million from the U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to assist Zimbabwean refugees and internally displaced persons. Furthermore, he emphasized that the United States will sustain its broader commitment to providing food and medical aid to the people of Zimbabwe.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN news article from July 2008 detailing President George W. Bush's executive order expanding U.S. sanctions against Robert Mugabe's regime in Zimbabwe.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON (CNN)** -- President George W. Bush signed an executive order Friday expanding U.S. sanctions against the regime of Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, targeting key state-owned companies and government officials following a deeply flawed and violent presidential runoff election.

The order freezes the U.S. assets of additional individuals and entities associated with Mugabe’s ruling party, ZANU-PF, and prohibits American citizens and businesses from engaging in financial transactions with them.

"No regime should be allowed to terrorize its own citizens," Bush said in a statement released by the White House. "The Mugabe regime has conducted a campaign of violence against its political opponents, making a mockery of the democratic process."

The move marks a significant escalation in Washington's effort to isolate Mugabe, who has ruled the southern African nation since its independence in 1980.

Among those targeted by the new Treasury Department sanctions are several prominent Zimbabwean state-owned enterprises, including the Zimbabwe Mining Development Corporation and the Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe, which serve as vital financial lifelines for the government. The order also penalizes individuals accused of organizing or participating in state-sponsored violence surrounding the June 27 election.

The expansion builds upon initial targeted sanctions first imposed by the Bush administration in 2003.

The crisis in Zimbabwe intensified sharply earlier this year. In March, opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai of the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) defeated Mugabe in the first round of the presidential vote, according to official results. However, election officials claimed Tsvangirai failed to win the absolute majority required to avoid a runoff.

In the weeks leading up to the June runoff, human rights organizations reported widespread political violence orchestrated by state security forces and pro-Mugabe militias. Dozens of opposition supporters were killed, thousands were injured, and MDC offices were raided. Citing the impossibility of a free and fair vote under such conditions, Tsvangirai withdrew from the race days before the ballot.

Mugabe proceeded with the uncontested election, declaring himself the winner and swiftly being sworn in for another term. The election was widely condemned by international observers, including the European Union, the United States, and several African nations.

"The results of the June 27 election are illegitimate," White House Press Secretary Dana Perino said Friday. "This executive order sends a clear message that the United States will hold accountable those who undermine democracy and human rights in Zimbabwe."

The U.S. action comes two weeks after Russia and China vetoed a United Nations Security Council resolution that would have imposed an international arms embargo and global sanctions on Mugabe and 13 of his top aides. U.S. officials indicated at the time that Washington would pursue unilateral sanctions alongside European allies in response to the veto.

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice applauded the new measures, calling on other nations to follow suit.

"The international community must stand united against the Mugabe regime’s illegal actions," Rice said in a statement. "We will continue to work with our partners in Africa and around the world to support the aspirations of the Zimbabwean people for genuine democracy and economic recovery."

Zimbabwe, once considered the breadbasket of southern Africa, has seen its economy collapse under Mugabe's tenure, marred by hyperinflation reaching millions of percent annually, widespread food shortages, and severe political instability.

Administration officials stated that the U.S. humanitarian aid to the people of Zimbabwe would not be affected by the expanded sanctions, emphasizing that the measures specifically target the regime's leadership and financial supporters.

*CNN's Ed Henry and Elise Labott contributed to this report.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you summarize the U.S. government's response to the 2008 election violence and political crisis in Zimbabwe?
counterfactuals.output:
The U.S. government’s response to the 2008 election violence and political crisis in Zimbabwe—led primarily by the administration of President George W. Bush, and transitioning into the Obama administration—was characterized by **strong diplomatic condemnation, targeted economic sanctions, multilateral pressure, and sustained humanitarian assistance.** 

The U.S. viewed the state-sponsored violence against the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) and the discredited June 2008 runoff election as a severe threat to democracy and human rights in southern Africa.

Here is a breakdown of the key elements of the U.S. response:

---

### 1. Diplomatic Condemnation and Non-Recognition
* **Rejection of Election Results:** The U.S. firmly rejected the legitimacy of the June 2008 presidential runoff, in which Robert Mugabe ran unopposed after MDC leader Morgan Tsvangirai withdrew due to widespread violence against his supporters. President Bush publicly called the runoff a "sham" and declared that the Mugabe regime was illegitimate.
* **Refusal to Recognize Mugabe:** Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice stated that the U.S. did not view Mugabe as the legitimate head of state and called for the international community to isolate his administration.

### 2. Expansion of Targeted Sanctions
Building on the Zimbabwe Democracy and Economic Recovery Act (ZIDERA) of 2001, the Bush administration intensified economic pressure against perpetrators of the violence:
* **Executive Order 13469 (July 2008):** President Bush signed an executive order expanding existing sanctions. This froze the U.S. assets of additional ZANU-PF officials, military personnel, state-owned enterprises, and private businesses/individuals that provided financial or material support to the violent crackdowns.
* **Targeted Focus:** The U.S. maintained that sanctions were "smart" or targeted specifically at regime elites and entities fueling human rights abuses, rather than the general Zimbabwean population.

### 3. Multilateral Diplomacy and the UN Security Council
* **UN Security Council Resolution:** In July 2008, the U.S. drafted and pushed for a legally binding UN Security Council resolution. The proposed resolution sought an international arms embargo on Zimbabwe, as well as a global travel ban and asset freeze on Mugabe and 13 senior officials.
* **The Veto:** Despite gaining majority support in the council, the resolution was vetoed by Russia and China. The U.S. strongly criticized both nations for protecting the Mugabe regime.
* **Pressure on Regional Bodies:** The U.S. repeatedly called on the African Union (AU) and the Southern African Development Community (SADC)—particularly South Africa’s President Thabo Mbeki—to take a firmer stance against Mugabe and facilitate a fair political settlement.

### 4. Continued Humanitarian Assistance
* **Bypassing the Regime:** Despite political tension and sanctions, the U.S. remained the largest single donor of humanitarian aid to the Zimbabwean people. 
* **Crisis Relief:** The U.S. provided hundreds of millions of dollars in emergency food relief, agricultural support, and health assistance, particularly during the devastating cholera outbreak that hit Zimbabwe in late 2008 and early 2009. Aid was funneled through non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and UN agencies to ensure it did not benefit the ZANU-PF government.

### 5. Reaction to the Power-Sharing Agreement (2008–2009)
When regional mediation led to the signing of the Global Political Agreement (GPA) and the formation of a Unity Government in early 2009—with Mugabe remaining President and Tsvangirai becoming Prime Minister—the U.S. (now under President Barack Obama) adopted a cautious stance:
* **"Wait and See" Policy:** The Obama administration welcomed the reduction in violence but stated it would not lift sanctions or provide direct financial aid to the government until there were concrete demonstrations of democratic reform, respect for human rights, and the rule of law.
* **Direct Support for Civil Society:** U.S. aid was directed toward supporting civil society, independent media, human rights defenders, and basic social services, avoiding direct funding to government institutions controlled by ZANU-PF.

---

### Summary
Overall, the U.S. government treated the 2008 crisis in Zimbabwe as a major democratic collapse. It responded by delegitimizing Robert Mugabe's government, punishing key perpetrators with expanded sanctions, advocating for global isolation of the regime, and maintaining direct humanitarian support for the population.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a detailed news report covering the U.S. Treasury Department's targeted sanctions against Zimbabwean state entities and foreign business associates like Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari, including quotes from the White House and background on UN Security Council vetoes.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON** — The U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated key Zimbabwean state-owned enterprises and foreign business intermediaries under its targeted sanctions regime, taking direct aim at international illicit financial networks accused of bankrolling state corruption and destabilizing the region. 

Among the high-profile individuals targeted in the enforcement action is Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari, an Omani national and prominent business associate of Zimbabwe's political and military elite. 

According to Treasury officials, al-Shanfari has leveraged a complex web of offshore companies—most notably Oryx Natural Resources—to facilitate illicit mineral exploitation and weaponize state assets for personal gain. The sanctions freeze all U.S.-based assets belonging to the designated individuals and entities and broadly prohibit American citizens and financial institutions from doing business with them.

### Target Network: Minerals and Military Power

Treasury documents detail how foreign facilitators like al-Shanfari acted as financial conduits for senior Zimbabwean officials, orchestrating opaque mining deals that bypassed national oversight. 

Al-Shanfari’s operations drew international scrutiny following United Nations reports highlighting the plunder of diamonds and other valuable resources from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) during and after the Second Congo War. Working in tandem with senior Zimbabwean military officers and state entities, al-Shanfari reportedly helped structure joint ventures that funneled millions of dollars away from public coffers and into private hands.

"For years, state-backed networks have stripped Zimbabwe of its vast wealth, relying on foreign facilitators to hide profits in secret bank accounts and shell companies," the White House said in a statement released Tuesday. "Today’s designations demonstrate our unwavering commitment to holding accountable those who profit from corruption and undermine the democratic aspirations of the Zimbabwean people."

The White House emphasized that the measures do not target the citizens of Zimbabwe. 

"Our sanctions are targeted directly at corrupt actors, abusive state entities, and their foreign accomplices," said a senior administration official during a White House briefing. "The economic hardship faced by ordinary Zimbabweans is the direct result of resource plunder and economic mismanagement by leadership, not the targeted restrictions placed on individuals who abuse the international financial system."

### Failure at the UN: The Shadow of the 2008 Veto

The U.S. relies heavily on unilateral executive orders—such as E.O. 13288 and subsequent modernizations—primarily because international consensus at the United Nations has been repeatedly blocked by rival superpowers.

The push for a unified, binding international response to corruption and political violence in Zimbabwe reached a critical nexus at the UN Security Council in July 2008. Following a violent, highly disputed presidential election, the United States and the United Kingdom drafted a landmark UN Security Council resolution proposing a global arms embargo, as well as targeted financial and travel restrictions against key government figures and associated business entities.

However, the resolution was dramatically defeated when Russia and China exercised a joint veto.

Moscow and Beijing argued at the time that Zimbabwe’s domestic political crisis did not constitute a threat to international peace and security, framing the resolution as an improper interference in sovereign internal affairs. The veto effectively killed any prospect of a multilateral UN sanctions regime, forcing Washington, Brussels, and London to build and enforce their own independent, targeted sanctions frameworks.

Diplomats note that the 2008 veto created a precedent that allowed international actors—including foreign nationals like al-Shanfari—to operate within the regulatory blind spots of non-Western jurisdictions. 

"The inability of the UN Security Council to act in 2008 left a void that state corruption networks quickly exploited," said Dr. Elena Rostova, a senior fellow at the Center for African Geopolitics. "Because a global framework was blocked, Washington has had to play a continuous game of financial whack-a-mole, updating its sanctions lists to target the foreign facilitators who keep these illicit financial pipelines flowing."

### Harare Responds

The government in Harare has consistently denounced all foreign sanctions, labeling them illegal "economic sabotage" intended to force regime change. Officials in Zimbabwe argue that the restrictions discourage broader foreign direct investment and penalize the nation's banking sector.

However, U.S. officials maintain that enforcement actions will continue to adapt to target modern financial evasion tactics. Treasury’s latest action serves as a warning to international business executives operating in the region: assisting sanctioned state entities or enriching autocratic leaders carries severe global financial consequences.

counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON / HARARE** — The Bush administration has announced a sweeping expansion of economic sanctions against the government of Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe today, escalating international pressure on the regime following a deeply flawed presidential runoff election that has plunged the Southern African nation into unprecedented political and economic turmoil.

The new measures, signed into effect via an executive order by President George W. Bush, target additional individuals and corporate entities linked to Mugabe’s inner circle. The move comes in response to months of state-sponsored violence aimed at suppressing political opposition, which ultimately forced opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai to withdraw from the June runoff election.

"The Mugabe regime has stolen an election from the people of Zimbabwe and used violence to maintain its grip on power," said a senior U.S. State Department official during a press briefing in Washington. "These targeted sanctions are designed to deny the regime's architects the ability to profit from their ill-gotten rule, while holding accountable those who enable political violence."

### An Election Marred by Violence

The diplomatic escalation follows the chaotic aftermath of Zimbabwe’s March 29 general election. In that contest, Tsvangirai and his party, the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), officially defeated Mugabe and the ruling ZANU-PF party. However, electoral authorities declared that Tsvangirai had failed to secure the 50 percent threshold required for an outright victory, forcing a presidential runoff scheduled for June 27.

In the weeks leading up to the runoff, Human Rights Watch and local observers documented a brutal, coordinated campaign of intimidation carried out by security forces and ZANU-PF youth militias. More than 80 opposition supporters were reportedly killed, thousands were beaten, and tens of thousands were displaced from their homes. 

On June 22, citing the systematic violence and the impossibility of a free and fair vote, Tsvangirai announced his agonizing decision to pull out of the race. "I cannot ask voters to cast their vote when that vote costs them their lives," Tsvangirai stated at a press conference in Harare shortly before seeking temporary refuge in the Dutch Embassy. 

Mugabe proceeded with the single-candidate runoff, taking the oath of office for another term despite widespread condemnation from the United Nations, the European Union, and the African Union.

### Targeted Sanctions vs. Humanitarian Relief

The newly announced U.S. sanctions specifically target the financial networks supporting ZANU-PF, including several state-owned enterprises and key figures within the military and intelligence sectors. The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has frozen all U.S.-based assets of these entities and prohibited American citizens and businesses from conducting transactions with them.

U.S. officials were quick to emphasize that the economic sanctions are targeted at regime elites, not the civilian population, which is currently enduring a catastrophic economic meltdown marked by hyperinflation estimated in the millions of percent, severe fuel shortages, and widespread unemployment.

To mitigate the suffering of ordinary citizens, Washington simultaneously reaffirmed its commitment to humanitarian relief. The U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) announced an additional commitment of emergency food and health aid, bringing total U.S. humanitarian assistance to Zimbabwe to over $200 million for the fiscal year. 

"Our fight is not with the people of Zimbabwe, who are suffering immensely," stated the State Department official. "We are expanding humanitarian aid to prevent widespread famine, even as we choke off the financial lifelines of their oppressors."

### The Role of Regional Diplomacy

As Washington tightens the financial vise, diplomatic efforts are shifting toward South Africa, which has been tasked by the Southern African Development Community (SADC) to mediate a resolution to the political stalemate. 

South African President Thabo Mbeki has faced intense international criticism—particularly from the U.S. and Great Britain—for his policy of "quiet diplomacy," which critics argue has shielded Mugabe from harsher international condemnation. However, Mbeki’s mediation remains the primary active diplomatic vehicle on the ground.

In recent days, representatives from both ZANU-PF and the MDC have convened in Pretoria under Mbeki’s auspices to negotiate a framework for power-sharing talks. The goal is to establish a transitional government that could stabilize the economy and pave the way for new, internationally monitored elections.

While Tsvangirai’s faction remains deeply skeptical of Mugabe’s willingness to cede actual power, the MDC leader acknowledged this week that political dialogue is the only path to prevent a complete national collapse. 

Western nations, including the U.S., have signaled that while they support a mediated political settlement, the expansion of sanctions will remain in place—and could be further broadened—until Mugabe's regime demonstrates a genuine commitment to democratic reform and an end to political persecution.

For now, the people of Zimbabwe remain caught between a brutal political crisis and an unrelenting economic catastrophe, waiting to see if regional diplomacy or international economic pressure can break the political deadlock in Harare.
